Try

¶
'''votive''' (vō′tiv), ''a.'' [< F. ''votif'' = Sp. Pg. It. ''votivo'', < L. ''votivus'', of or pertaining to a vow, conformable to one’s wish, < ''votum'', vow: see ''vote'', ''vow''.] '''1.''' Offered, contributed, or consecrated in accordance with a vow: as, a ''votive'' picture.
{{smaller block|<poem>
Not gold, not blood, their altar dowers,
But ''votive'' tears and symbol flowers.</poem>
{{right|''Shelley'', Hellas.}}
<poem>
We set to-day a ''votive'' stone,
That memory may their dead redeem,
When, like our sires, our sons are gone.</poem>
{{right|''Emerson'', Concord Monument.}}
''Votive'' tablets commemorative of cures and deliverance were hung around.
{{right|''C. E. Norton'', Travel and Study in Italy, p. 232.}}}}
'''2.''' Observed, practised, or done in consequence of a vow. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|''Votive'' abstinence some cold constitutions may endure.
{{right|''Feltham'', Resolves, i. 85.}}
Diversions of this kind have a practical value, even though they seem to be those of a knight tilting at a wayside tournament as he rides on his ''votive'' quest.
{{right|''Stedman'', Vict. Poets, p. 399.}}}}
{{smaller|'''Votive mass.''' See ''mass''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Votive offering,''' a tablet, picture, or the like dedicated in fulfilment of the vow (Latin ''ex voto'') of a worshiper. Among the Greeks and Romans such offerings were dedicated to deities or heroes, and were affixed to the walls of temples, or set up in consecrated places, often in niches cut in the rock in a locality reputed sacred. Among Roman Catholics they are usually set up in chapels dedicated to the Virgin or to a saint.}}

'''votively''' (vō′tiv-li), ''adv.'' In a votive manner; by vow.

¶
'''votiveness''' (vō′tiv-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being votive.

'''votress†''' (vō′tres), ''n.'' Same as ''votaress.''

'''vouch''' (vouch), ''v.'' [< ME. ''vouchen'', ''vowchen'', < OF. ''voucher'', ''vocher'', < L. ''vocare'', call, call upon, summon: see ''vocation'', ''voice.'' Cf. ''vouchsafe'', ''avouch.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1†.''' To call to witness.
{{smaller block|And ''vouch'' the silent stars, and conscious moon.
{{right|''Dryden'', tr. of Ovid’s Metamorph., xiii. 22.}}}}
'''2.''' To declare; assert; affirm; attest; avouch.
{{smaller block|Praised therefore be his name, which ''voucheth'' us worthy this honour.
{{right|''J. Bradford'', Letters (Parker Soc., 1853), II. 176.}}
What can you ''vouch'' against him, Signior Lucio?
{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., v. 1. 326.}}
<poem>
. What we have done
None shall dare ''vouch'', though it be truly known.
</poem>
{{right|''Shelley'', Revolt of Islam, ix. 31.}}}}
'''3.''' To warrant; be surety for; answer for; make good; confirm.
{{smaller block|<poem>
Go tell the lords o’ the city I am here;
Deliver them this paper; having read it,
Bid them repair to the market-place, where I,
Even in theirs and in the commons’ ears,
Will ''vouch'' the truth of it.
</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Cor., v. 6. 5.}}
When I arrived at Scutari, they took my slave from me, as I had not the original writing by me to ''vouch'' the property of him. ''Pococke'', Description of the East, II. ii. 126.}}
'''4.''' To support; back; second; follow up. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Bold words ''vouch’d'' with a deed so bold.
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., v. 66.}}}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|vote|6791|vow}}</noinclude>{{nop}}{{smaller block|It is of no use to ''vote down'' gravitation or morals.
{{right|''Emerson'', Fugitive Slave Law.}}}}

{{smaller|'''To vote in,''' to choose by suffrage; elect, as to an appointment or office, by expression of will or preference: as, he was ''voted in'' by a handsome majority.}}

'''voteless''' (vōt′les), ''a.''   [< ''vote'' + ''-less.'']   Having no vote; not entitled to a vote.
{{smaller block|He was not enlightened enough to know that there was a way of using ''voteless'' miners and navvies at Nominations and Elections.
{{right|''George Eliot'', Felix Holt, xi.}}}}

'''voter''' (vō′tėr), ''n.''   [< ''vote'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   One who votes or has a legal right to vote; an elector.
{{smaller block|Of late years, . . . when it has been considered necessary by politicians to cultivate the foreign-born ''voters'', there has been a great tendency to appoint naturalized citizens as consuls.
{{right|''Schuyler'', Amer. Diplomacy, p. 81.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Registration of voters.''' See ''registration.''}}

'''vote-recorder''' (vōt′rẹ̄-kôr″dėr), ''n.'' An electrical device which records the yea or nay of a voter when the corresponding knob or button is pressed.

'''voting-paper''' (vō′ting-pā″pėr), ''n.'' A balloting-paper; particularly, according to the British Ballot Act of 1872, a paper used in voting by ballot in the election of members of Parliament, of municipal corporations, etc. {{smaller|Such papers are used only in cases where the number of candidates exceeds the number of vacancies; they contain a list of the candidates, and the voter is required to put a mark opposite the name of each candidate he selects.}}

'''votist†''' (vō′tist), ''n.''   [< L. ''votum'', vow, + ''-ist.'']   One who makes a vow; a vower; a votarist.
<poem>
Try
If a poor woman, ''votist'' of revenge,
Would not perform it.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Chapman'', Revenge of Bussy D’Ambois, iii. 1.}}}}

'''votive''' (vō′tiv), ''a.''   [< F. ''votif'' = Sp. Pg. It. ''votivo'', < L. ''votivus'', of or pertaining to a vow, conformable to one’s wish, < ''votum'', vow: see ''vote'', ''vow''.]   '''1.''' Offered, contributed, or consecrated in accordance with a vow: as, a ''votive'' picture.
{{smaller block|<poem>
Not gold, not blood, their altar dowers,
But ''votive'' tears and symbol flowers.</poem>
{{right|''Shelley'', Hellas.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>
We set to-day a ''votive'' stone,
That memory may their dead redeem,
When, like our sires, our sons are gone.</poem>
{{right|''Emerson'', Concord Monument.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Votive'' tablets commemorative of cures and deliverance were hung around.
{{right|''C. E. Norton'', Travel and Study in Italy, p. 232.}}}}
'''2.''' Observed, practised, or done in consequence of a vow. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|''Votive'' abstinence some cold constitutions may endure.
{{right|''Feltham'', Resolves, i. 85.}}}}
{{smaller block|Diversions of this kind have a practical value, even though they seem to be those of a knight tilting at a wayside tournament as he rides on his ''votive'' quest.
{{right|''Stedman'', Vict. Poets, p. 399.}}}}
{{smaller|'''Votive mass.''' See ''mass''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Votive offering,''' a tablet, picture, or the like dedicated in fulfilment of the vow (Latin ''ex voto'') of a worshiper. Among the Greeks and Romans such offerings were dedicated to deities or heroes, and were affixed to the walls of temples, or set up in consecrated places, often in niches cut in the rock in a locality reputed sacred. Among Roman Catholics they are usually set up in chapels dedicated to the Virgin or to a saint.}}

'''votively''' (vō′tiv-li), ''adv.'' In a votive manner; by vow.

'''votiveness''' (vō′tiv-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being votive.

'''votress†''' (vō′tres), ''n.'' Same as ''votaress.''

'''vouch''' (vouch), ''v.''   [< ME. ''vouchen'', ''vowchen'', < OF. ''voucher'', ''vocher'', < L. ''vocare'', call, call upon, summon: see ''vocation'', ''voice.'' Cf. ''vouchsafe'', ''avouch.'']   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1†.''' To call to witness.
{{smaller block|And ''vouch'' the silent stars, and conscious moon.
{{right|''Dryden'', tr. of Ovid’s Metamorph., xiii. 22.}}}}
'''2.''' To declare; assert; affirm; attest; avouch.
{{smaller block|Praised therefore be his name, which ''voucheth'' us worthy this honour.
{{right|''J. Bradford'', Letters (Parker Soc., 1853), II. 176.}}}}
{{smaller block|What can you ''vouch'' against him, Signior Lucio?
{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., v. 1. 326.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>
. What we have done
None shall dare ''vouch'', though it be truly known.
</poem>
{{right|''Shelley'', Revolt of Islam, ix. 31.}}}}
'''3.''' To warrant; be surety for; answer for; make good; confirm.
{{smaller block|<poem>
Go tell the lords o’ the city I am here;
Deliver them this paper; having read it,
Bid them repair to the market-place, where I,
Even in theirs and in the commons’ ears,
Will ''vouch'' the truth of it.
</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Cor., v. 6. 5.}}}}
{{smaller block|When I arrived at Scutari, they took my slave from me, as I had not the original writing by me to ''vouch'' the property of him.
{{right|''Pococke'', Description of the East, II. ii. 126.}}}}
'''4.''' To support; back; second; follow up. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Bold words ''vouch’d'' with a deed so bold.
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., v. 66.}}}} '''5.''' In ''law:'' (''a'') To produce vouchers for, in support of a charge in account. (''b'') In ''old Eng. law'', to call or summon into court to warrant and defend, or to make good a warranty of title.
{{smaller block|He ''vouches'' the tenant in tail, who ''vouches'' over the common vouchee.
{{right|''Blackstone'', Com., II. xxi.}}}}
='''Syn. 2.''' {{smaller|To asseverate, aver, protest.}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To bear witness; give testimony or attestation; more specifically, in ''old Eng. law'', to call in some one to make good his alleged warranty of title; be surety or guaranty.
{{smaller block|''Vouch'' with me, heaven.
{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, i. 3. 262.}}}}
{{smaller block|The Salvo of Sir John Friendly’s appearing at last, and ''vouching'' for Lord Foplington, won’t mend the matter.
{{right|''Jeremy Collier'', Short View (ed. 1698), p. 215.}}}}
{{smaller block|A very clear account, upon my word; and I dare swear the lady will ''vouch'' for every article of it.
{{right|''Sheridan'', School for Scandal, iv. 3.}}}}

{{smaller block|'''To vouch to warranty''', in ''old Eng. law'', to call in a third person as a substituted defendant, to defend the title acquired from him. ='''Syn.''' Of ''vouch for'', warrant, assure, guarantee.}}

'''vouch''' (vouch), ''n.''   [< ''vouch'', ''v.'']   Approving or supporting warrant; confirmation; attestation.
{{smaller block|<poem>Why in this woolvish toge should I stand here,
To beg of Hob and Dick, that do appear,
Their needless ''vouches?'' {{right|''Shak.'', Cor., ii. 3. 124.}}</poem>}}

'''vouchee''' (vou-chē′), ''n.''   [< ''vouch'' + ''-ee''<sup>1</sup>.]   In ''law'', the person who is vouched or summoned in a writ of right.
{{smaller block|All trouble on this score was avoided by choosing as ''vouchee'' some one who notoriously had no lands to make recompense withal, and therefore was, as we now say, not worth powder and shot.
{{right|''F. Pollock'', Land Laws, p. 31.}}}}

'''voucher''' (vou′chėr), ''n.''   [< ''vouch'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' One who vouches, or gives attestation or confirmation; one who is surety for another.
{{smaller block|He knows his own strength so well that he never dares praise anything in which he has not a French author for his ''voucher''.
{{right|''Addison'', Tatler, No. 165.}}}}
{{smaller block|Some banks will not take the accounts of persons introduced only by their own clerks, for fear they might be confederates in some scheme of fraud or plunder. Other and responsible ''vouchers'' are required.
{{right|''Harper’s Mag.'', LXXX. 468.}}}}
'''2.''' A book, paper, document, or stamp which serves to prove the truth of accounts, or to confirm and establish facts of any kind; specifically, a receipt or other written evidence of the payment of money.
{{smaller block|The stamp is a mark, . . . and a public ''voucher'', that a piece of such denomination is of such a weight.
{{right|''Locke'', Further Considerations concerning Raising the [Value of Money.}}}}
{{smaller block|He caused the accounts to be examined by the proper officer, who, after comparing every article with its ''voucher'', certified them to be right.
{{right|''Franklin'', Autobiog., p. 260.}}}}
'''3.''' In ''old Eng. law'': (''a'') The tenant in a writ of right; one who called in another to establish his warranty of title. In common recoveries there might be a single voucher or double vouchers. [Also written ''vouchor.''] (''b'') The calling in of a person to vouch.—{{smaller|'''Double voucher,''' an incident in the alienation of land by the fiction of common recovery, where the owner was allowed to convey to a third person who, being sued, alleged that the former warranted the title, and he, being called to vouch for it, was allowed to allege that still another warranted it to him, the object being to bar contingent interests, etc.}}

'''vouchment''' (vouch′ment), ''n.''   [< ''vouch'' + ''-ment.'']   A declaration or affirmation; a solemn assertion.
{{smaller block|Their ''vouchment'' by their honour in that tryal is not an oath. {{right|''Bp. Hacket,'' Abp. Williams, i. 77. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''vouchor''' (vou′cho̤r), ''n.''   [< ''vouch'' + ''-or''<sup>1</sup>.]   See ''voucher'', 3 (''a'').

'''vouchsafe''' (vouch-sāf′), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''vouchsafed'', ppr. ''vouchsafing''.   [< ME. ''vouchen safe'', ''saf'', ''sauf'', prop. two words, lit. ‘guarantee (as) safe’; < ''vouch'' + ''safe.'']   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1†.''' To guarantee as safe; secure; assure.
{{smaller block|<poem>That the quen be of-sent, ''sauf'' wol i ''fouche.''</poem>
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 4152.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>So Philip is wild, on that wise we it take
As ge haf mad present, the kyng ''vouches'' it ''saue.''</poem>
{{right|''Rob. of Brunne,'' p. 260. (''Richardson.'')}}}}
'''2.''' To permit, grant, or bestow: sometimes with implied condescension: as, not to ''vouchsafe'' an answer.
{{smaller block|I have assailed her with music, but she ''vouchsafes'' no notice. {{right|''Shak.,'' Cymbeline, ii. 3. 45.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>In your pardon, and the kiss ''vouchsafed'' me,
You did but point me out a fore-right way
To lead to certain happiness.</poem>
{{right|''Massinger,'' Parliament of Love, iii. 3.}}}}

{{smaller block|Sir, I must thank you for the Visit you ''vouchsafed'' me in this simple Cell.
{{right|''Howell'', Letters, ii. 69.}}}}

'''3†.''' To receive or accept by way of condescension.
{{smaller block|There she sate, ''vouchsafing'' my cloak (then most gorgeous) under her.
{{right|''Sir P. Sidney'', Arcadia, i.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Upon which better part our prayers come in,
If thou ''vouchsafe'' them.</poem>{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, iii. 1. 294.}}}}
'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To permit; grant; condescend; deign; stoop.
{{smaller block|Than he preyede devoutly to God, that he wolde ''vouche saf'' to suffre him gon up.{{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 149.}}}}
{{smaller block|God ''vouched sauf'' thurgh thee with us to acorde.{{right|''Chaucer'', A. B. C., l. 27.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Vouchsafe'', noble Lady, to accept this simple remembrance.{{right|''Spenser'', Tears of the Muses, Ded.}}}}

'''vouchsafement''' (vouch-sāf′ment), ''n.''   [< ''vouchsafe'' + ''-ment''.]   The act of vouchsafing, or that which is vouchsafed; a gift or grant in condescension. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Peculiar experiences being such ''vouchsafements'' to them, which God communicated to none but his chosen people.
{{right|''Stillingfleet'', Sermons, I. viii.}}}}

'''voudou, voudouism.''' See ''voodoo, voodooism.''

'''vouge''' (vözh), ''n.'' Same as ''voulge.''

'''vough,''' ''n.'' Same as ''vug.''

'''voulge''' (vözh), ''n.''   [< OF. ''voulge, vouge, voouge,'' F. ''vouge'' (ML. ''vanga''), a hunting-spear, a lance; origin unknown.]   A weapon consisting of a blade fitted on a long handle or staff, used by the foot-soldiers of the fourteenth century and later. {{smaller|It varied in form, resembling sometimes the fauchard, sometimes the war-scythe, sometimes the halberd, and was frequently like an ax the blade of which, with but slight projection, has great length in the direction of the staff, and is finished at the end in a sharp point.}}

'''vound†,''' ''a.'' An unexplained word, perhaps a mistake for ''round,'' occurring in the following passage:
{{smaller block|<poem>Though it were of no ''vounde'' stone,
Wrought with squyre and scantilone.</poem>
{{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 7063.}}}} {{img float|file=century v08 p0595 c3f1.png|width=109px|align=right|cap={{smaller|Voulge of the end of the 14th century. (From Viollet-le-Duc’s “Dict. du Mobilier français.”)}}}}

'''vour†,''' ''v. t.''   [ME. ''vourer,'' < OF. *''vourer, vorer,'' < L. ''vorare,'' devour, eat; cf. ''vora'''cious, devour.''''']<!-- --> To devour.

{{smaller block|Thei whom the sward deuowrede [var. ''vowrede''].
{{right|''Wyclif,'' 2 Ki. [2 Sam.] xviii. 8.}}}}

'''vourer†''', ''n.'' A devourer.

{{smaller block|Lo! a man deuourere, ether glotoun [var. ''vourer'' or glotoun].
{{right|''Wyclif,'' Luke vii. 34.}}}}

'''voussoir''' (vö-swor′), ''n.''   [F.; cf. ''voussure,'' the curvature of a vault, prop. < *''vousser,'' < LL. as if *''volutiare,'' make round, < L. ''volutus,'' a rolling, < ''volvere,'' pp. ''volutus,'' roll: see ''volute.'']   In ''arch.,'' a stone in the shape of a truncated wedge, which forms part of an arch. {{smaller|The under sides of the voussoirs form the intrados or soffit of the arch, and the upper sides the extrados. The middle voussoir is often termed the ''keystone.'' See ''arch''<sup>1</sup>, 2.}}

'''voussoir''' (vö-swor′), ''v. t.''   [< ''voussoir, n.'']   To form with voussoirs; construct by means of voussoirs. ''Encyc. Brit.,'' II. 387.

'''voute†''', ''n.'' An obsolete form of ''vault''<sup>1</sup>.

'''voutre†''', '''voutur†''', ''n.'' Obsolete forms of ''vulture.''

'''vow''' (vou), ''n.''   [< ME. ''vow,'' < OF. ''vou, vo, veu,'' F. ''vœu'' = Sp. Pg. It. ''voto,'' a vow, < L. ''votum,'' a promise, dedication, vow, < ''vovere,'' promise, vow: see ''vote, n.,'' of which ''vow'' is a doublet.]   '''1.''' A solemn promise; an engagement solemnly entered into. {{smaller|Specifically—(''a'') A kind of promissory oath made to God, or to some deity, to perform some act or dedicate to the deity something of value, often in the event of receiving something specially desired, such as success in an enterprise, deliverance from danger, or recovery from sickness: as, a ''vow'' to build an altar.}}

<poem>Would I were even the saint they make their ''vows'' to!
How easily I would grant! {{right|''Fletcher,'' Pilgrim, i. 2.}}</poem>
{{smaller block|Forc’d Consecrations out of another mans Estate are no better than forc’d ''Vows,'' hateful to God who loves a chearful giver.
{{right|''Milton,'' Touching Hirelings.}}}}

{{smaller block|A ''vow'' is a deliberate promise made to God in regard to something possessing superior goodness. To be valid, it must proceed from the free, deliberate will of one who, by age and social position, is capable of contracting a solemn obligation. It is to God alone that a ''vow'' is taken, and . . . it is an act of religion, or of divine worship. To vow to a saint means, in the minds of Catholics, to vow to God in honour of a saint. {{right|''Rom. Cath. Dict.''}}}}

(''b'') A promise to follow out some line of conduct, or to consecrate or devote one’s self wholly or in part for a longer or shorter time to some act or service; a pledge of fidelity or constancy: as, a marriage ''vow''.
{{smaller block|<poem>Fooles therefore
They are which fortunes doe by ''vowes'' devize,
Sith each unto himselfe his life may fortunize.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., VI. ix. 30.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>By all the ''vows'' that ever men have broke,
In number more than ever women spoke.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. N. D., i. 1. 175.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
